العدالة في السودان الإثنين من احتمال تكرار فظائع «واسعة النطاق» في البلاد، كتلك التي ارتُكبت عندما سيطرت قوات «الدعم السريع» على الفاشر قبل عام. وقالت ألمانيا وكندا والدنمارك وإيرلندا وفرنسا والنروج وهولندا والمملكة المتحدة وسيراليون والسويد والاتحاد الأوروبي في بيان مشترك «في 26 تشرين الأول/أكتوبر 2025، بلغ العنف في الفاشر ومحيطها ذروة مدمّرة بعد أشهر من الحصار والهجمات المتصاعدة التي شنّتها قوات الدعم السريع»، التي تخوض حربا ضدّ الجيش السوداني. وأضافت «تعرّض مدنيون لفظائع مروّعة شملت مجازر وعمليات قتل على أساس الانتماء الإثني وإعدامات ميدانية وتعذيبا وحالات اختفاء وتجنيدا قسريا واعتقالات تعسفية، فضلا عن انتشار واسع للعنف الجنسي والعنف القائم على النوع الاجتماعي». واعتبر خبراء في الأمم المتحدة أنّ الهجوم الذي شنّته قوات الدعم السريع للسيطرة على آخر مدينة كبرى في دارفور (غرب) كانت لا تزال بيد الجيش، حمل «سمات إبادة جماعية». وفي ظلّ الحرب المستعرة منذ نيسان/أبريل 2023 بين الجيش بقيادة عبد الفتاح البرهان وقوات الدعم السريع بقيادة محمد حمدان دقلو المعروف بحميدتي، أكّدت الدول في البيان أن «خطر وقوع فظائع جديدة واسعة النطاق في السودان لا يزال مرتفعا للغاية»، مشيرة إلى تزايد استخدام الطائرات المسيّرة. بريطانيا تفرض عقوبات على 15 قيادياً بسبب مجازر الفاشر وقال الموقّعون إن هذه الذكرى المأسوية «تذكّرنا بضرورة العمل معا لمنع تكرار ما حدث». وأضافوا «ندعو أيضا جميع الدول إلى احترام القانون الدولي واستخدام نفوذها لحماية المدنيين ومنع وقوع فظائع جديدة والمساهمة في إنهاء هذا النزاع المدمّر». وتزامنا مع البيان، فرضت المملكة المتحدة، الإثنين، عقوبات على 15 من كبار القيادات العسكرية والميدانية المرتبطة بالحرب في السودان، للاشتباه في تورطهم في ارتكاب انتهاكات جسيمة بحق المدنيين. وتشمل العقوبات قيادات من قوات الدعم السريع والقوات المسلحة السودانية، إلى جانب شخصيات مرتبطة بتشكيلات مسلحة. وتتضمن الإجراءات حظر السفر إلى المملكة المتحدة وتجميد الأصول المالية، بما يمنع المشمولين بها من الوصول إلى الأموال والموارد الاقتصادية الخاضعة للاختصاص البريطاني. ومن بين الأسماء التي أعلنتها الحكومة البريطانية حسين أبو جلك، وهو عقيد في قوات الدعم السريع، للاشتباه في ارتباطه بانتهاكات ارتكبت خلال حصار الفاشر والهجوم عليها. كما تشمل النور أحمد آدم «القبة»، الذي تقول السلطات البريطانية إنه كان موجوداً في المدينة وأدى دوراً بارزاً في حصارها والهجوم عليها. وقالت الحكومة البريطانية إن الإجراءات تستهدف تسليط الضوء على ما شهدته الفاشر، وضمان بقاء الانتهاكات المبلغ عنها موثقة ومعروفة دولياً، مؤكدة أن مرتكبي الفظائع ينبغي أن يخضعوا للمساءلة. وأشارت إلى توثيق أنماط من التجويع المتعمد والعنف الجنسي المرتبط بالنزاع، مع الإشارة إلى انتهاكات ارتكبتها أطراف مختلفة في الحرب السودانية. اترك تعليقاً إلغاء الرد لن يتم نشر عنوان بريدك الإلكتروني. الحقول الإلزامية مشار إليها لهجمات بطائرات مسيرة، شملت سنجة والحواتة والفاو ومشكور والجنيد، ما أدى إلى أضرار في منشآت الكهرباء وانقطاع التيار عن أجزاء واسعة من ولايات سنار والقضارف والنيل الأبيض والجزيرة. وقالت الشركة إن الهجمات التي نفذتها قوات الدعم استهدفت محطات كهربائية في مناطق متفرقة من البلاد، وأدت إلى خروج عدد منها عن الخدمة، الأمر الذي انعكس على استقرار الشبكة الكهربائية والإمدادات في الولايات المتأثرة. وأشارت إلى تحرك الفرق الفنية والهندسية لحصر الأضرار والعمل على معالجة الأعطال وإعادة التيار. وفي ولاية القضارف شرق السودان، سمع المواطنون دوي انفجارات قوية بينما تصاعدت ألسنة اللهب، من محطتي الكهرباء في الفاو والحواتة التي هاجمتها مسيرات الدعم خلال الساعات الأولى من صباح الإثنين، ما أدى إلى خروج الشبكة الشرقية من الخدمة وحدوث إظلام تام. وفي ولاية سنار، جنوب شرق البلاد، أعلنت لجنة أمن الولاية أن محطة سنجة التحويلية تعرضت لهجوم بطائرة مسيرة استراتيجية أطلقت صاروخين على المحطة، ما أسفر عن أضرار مادية وإصابة عدد من أفراد طاقم الحراسة. أجزاء من 4 ولايات غرقت في الظلام وأوضحت اللجنة أن المصابين نقلوا لتلقي الرعاية الطبية، فيما شرعت الفرق الفنية المختصة في إجراء حصر دقيق وشامل للأضرار والخسائر التي لحقت بالمحطة. وأضافت أن لجنة أمن الولاية نفذت زيارة تفقدية للموقع ووقفت على حجم الأضرار، مؤكدة أن الأوضاع في الولاية تحت السيطرة، وداعية المواطنين إلى عدم الانسياق وراء الشائعات والمعلومات المضللة. وامتدت الهجمات حسب شركة الكهرباء السودانية، إلى محطة مشكور في ولاية النيل الأبيض جنوب البلاد ومحطة الجنيد في ولاية الجزيرة وسط البلاد، إلى جانب محطتي الفاو والحواتة في القضارف الواقعة شرقا ومحطة سنجة في سنار جنوب شرق البلاد. وفي ولاية الجزيرة، تعرضت محطة الجنيد التحويلية للاستهداف خلال الساعات الأولى من صباح الإثنين، ما أدى إلى أضرار وخروج المحطة عن الخدمة، وانعكاس ذلك على إمدادات الكهرباء في المناطق المرتبطة بها. كما تعرضت محطة مشكور للاستهداف في التوقيت نفسه. ويمثل انقطاع الكهرباء تحدياً إضافياً للسكان في الولايات المتأثرة، في ظل الظروف الإنسانية والاقتصادية الصعبة التي تعيشها البلاد منذ اندلاع الحرب. ولا تقتصر آثار انقطاع التيار على المنازل والأنشطة التجارية، بل تمتد إلى تشغيل محطات ضخ المياه والمخابز والمرافق الصحية ومراكز الاتصالات، فضلاً عن الأنشطة الزراعية والصناعية التي تعتمد على الطاقة الكهربائية بصورة مباشرة أو غير مباشرة. وتتهم السلطات السودانية قوات الدعم السريع باستهداف منشآت الكهرباء والوقود وغيرها من المرافق المدنية والخدمية، وتقول إن هذه الهجمات تهدف إلى تعطيل الخدمات وإلحاق أضرار بالبنية التحتية. وأكدت شركة كهرباء السودان استنفار فرقها الهندسية والفنية لحصر الأضرار التي لحقت بالمحطات المستهدفة، واتخاذ الإجراءات اللازمة لإعادة الخدمة واستقرار الشبكة الكهربائية. كلمات مفتاحية ميعاد مبارك اترك تعليقاً إلغاء الرد لن يتم نشر عنوان بريدك الإلكتروني. الحقول الإلزامية السودان 0 تلاميذ في فصل دراسي مدمر جزئياً في مدرسة بولاية الخرطوم.. 13 مايو 2026 "يونيسف" الخرطوم 26 أكتوبر 2026 – رسمت منظمة كير الدولية، الاثنين، صورة قاتمة لمستقبل التعليم في السودان ، حيث تفتقر معظم المدارس إلى مياه الشرب والصرف الصحي، وسط حرمان 8 ملايين طفل من الدراسة. وتسعى السلطات إلى إعادة الأطفال إلى المدارس التي تعرضت لـ67 هجومًا منذ عام 2024، وفقًا للأمم المتحدة، التي تقول إنه جرى الإبلاغ عن 154 حالة استخدام عسكري لمرافق التعليم. وقالت منظمة كير، في تقرير، إن “نحو 8 ملايين طفل لا يحصلون على أي شكل من أشكال التعليم داخل الفصول الدراسية، بينما تأثر أو انقطع تعليم نحو 19 إلى 19.5 مليون طفل، وفق تقديرات يونيسف ومنظمة التعليم لا ينتظر”. وكشفت عن إعادة فتح أبواب 12,243 مدرسة من أصل 19,883 مدرسة، حيث ارتفعت نسبة إعادة فتح المدارس على المستوى الوطني من 32% في أبريل 2025 إلى نحو 62% بحلول مايو 2026. وأفادت بأن إعادة فتح المدارس لا تعني بالضرورة قدرتها على استقبال التلاميذ، نظرًا إلى أن العديد منها يعاني الاكتظاظ ونقص المقاعد والمواد الدراسية والمياه والمعلمين، فضلًا عن المخاطر الأمنية ومخاطر الحماية. وأوضح التقرير أن نسب إعادة فتح المدارس تتفاوت بصورة كبيرة بين الولايات، حيث لم تتجاوز 3% في شمال دارفور، و13% في جنوب دارفور، و15% في غرب كردفان، التي تشهد أعلى معدلات التسرب من المدارس، بنسبة تصل إلى 88%. وأشار إلى أن شمال دارفور تتصدر قائمة الولايات الأكثر تضررًا في الوصول إلى التعليم، حيث لم تُفتح سوى 33 مدرسة من أصل 1,118 مدرسة، فيما بلغ عدد الأطفال المحتاجين إلى التعليم 1.13 مليون طفل، بينما وصل عدد الأطفال خارج المدرسة إلى 1.09 مليون طفل. وبيّن أنه رغم إعادة فتح 13% من مدارس جنوب دارفور، فإن الولاية تضم 1.09 مليون طفل خارج المدرسة، فيما بلغ عدد الأطفال خارج المدرسة في شرق دارفور نحو 482 ألفًا، مع فرض 89% من مدارسها رسومًا دراسية. وذكر التقرير أن شمال كردفان سجلت أكبر عدد من الأطفال المحتاجين إلى التعليم على مستوى السودان، بواقع 1.19 مليون طفل. وقال إن عدد الأطفال خارج المدرسة في الخرطوم بلغ 833,018 طفلًا، بما يمثل 61.1% من الأطفال في سن الدراسة، مع تراجع الالتحاق بالتعليم الثانوي إلى 13% من مستواه قبل الحرب. واستند تقرير منظمة كير، الذي غطى جميع ولايات السودان، إلى مراجعة منظمة لـ72 وثيقة، إضافة إلى مقابلات مع موظفي منظمات محلية ودولية ووكالتين تابعتين للأمم المتحدة، علاوة على محادثات مع مسؤولين حكوميين ومديري مدارس. أسباب أخرى وتحدث التقرير عن تراجع خدمات المياه والصرف الصحي والنظافة والتغذية المدرسية، مشيرًا إلى أن 202 مدرسة فقط من أصل 19,883 مدرسة مزودة بشبكة مياه للشرب. وقال إن 55 مدرسة فقط في السودان مزودة بمرافق لغسل اليدين، بينما بلغ عدد المدارس التي تحتوي على دورات مياه 22 مدرسة، فيما تُظهر البيانات الأساسية أن معدلات إكمال الفتيات للتعليم تنخفض إلى النصف في المناطق التي تفتقر إلى دورات المياه. وذكر أن النزوح أعاد تشكيل خريطة الطلب على التعليم، نظرًا إلى استقبال ولايات وسط وشرق البلاد موجات متتالية من الأسر النازحة والعائدة، بينما فقدت ولايات دارفور وكردفان أعدادًا كبيرة من المدارس والمعلمين والسجلات الإدارية. وأوضح أن عدد التلاميذ في الفصل الواحد في عطبرة بولاية نهر النيل ارتفع من 70 إلى 80 تلميذًا قبل الحرب إلى ما بين 150 و180 تلميذًا بعد النزوح، كما تحولت مدارس في ولاية البحر الأحمر إلى مراكز إيواء، ما أدى إلى تعطيل الدراسة. وكشفت منظمة كير عن استخدام 18% من المدارس على المستوى الوطني مراكز إيواء للنازحين، الأمر الذي يحرم الأطفال من التعليم حتى في المناطق التي لم تتعرض فيها المباني المدرسية للتدمير. العنف ضد الأطفال وقال التقرير إن الحرب فاقمت مخاطر تجنيد الأطفال وعمالتهم والعنف القائم على النوع الاجتماعي والزواج المبكر، بالتزامن مع فقدان فرص التعليم. واستشهد بتقديرات وثقتها الأمم المتحدة تفيد بتجنيد 234 طفلًا من قبل جهات مسلحة، وتعرض 187 فتاة للعنف الجنسي خلال عامي 2023 و2024. وأوضح أن الأطفال الذين لا يحصلون على التعليم يصبحون أكثر عرضة للتجنيد والعمل القسري والزواج المبكر، ما يؤدي إلى تداخل الأزمة التعليمية مع أزمة الحماية. وأشار إلى أن قضايا النوع الاجتماعي والإعاقة والضغوط النفسية والاجتماعية واحتياجات الأطفال الذين تجاوزوا أعمار الصفوف الدراسية، والأطفال الرحل والرعاة، تمثل تحديات مشتركة في مختلف محاور التعليم. وسلط التقرير الضوء على الأجور، مشيرًا إلى أن رواتب المعلمين ظلت غير مدفوعة أو مدفوعة بصورة جزئية لمدة تتراوح بين 3 و4 سنوات، كما دفع ضعف الحوافز بعض المعلمين إلى مغادرة المهنة. وبيّن أن توقف قدرات الطباعة الوطنية خلال الحرب أدى إلى تقييد إنتاج الكتب والمواد التعليمية، ما يجعل معالجة النقص مرتبطة بتوفير حلول للإنتاج والشراء والتوزيع معًا. ويتطلب إنقاذ قطاع التعليم في البلاد تمويلًا يشمل زيادة رواتب المعلمين، وتوفير المستلزمات التعليمية، وترميم المدارس، ونقل النازحين المقيمين في مرافق التعليم إلى مواقع بديلة. الكلمات: أجور المعلمين أزمة التعليم السودان الانتهاكات التغذية فيها ضريبة القيمة المضافة، إلى جانب إلغاء حظر استيراد بعض السلع الغذائية وغيرها، في خطوة تستهدف تخفيف أعباء المعيشة وتوفير السلع للمواطنين. وتشهد الأسواق السودانية ارتفاعاً متواصلاً في أسعار السلع الاستهلاكية، مدفوعاً باستمرار تراجع قيمة الجنيه السوداني وارتفاع تكاليف ترحيل البضائع بين الولايات، بالتزامن مع شح الوقود. وقال إعلام مجلس الوزراء، في بيان صحفي الاثنين، إن قائمة السلع المعفاة تشمل الدقيق والعدس والأرز والفول المصري وزيوت الطعام والفاصوليا والحمص والبسلة. ولم يحدد البيان أسماء السلع الأخرى التي يشملها قرار إلغاء حظر الاستيراد، فيما وجّه وزارتي المالية والصناعة والتجارة، وقوات الجمارك، وجهاز المخابرات العامة، والجهات المعنية الأخرى، باتخاذ الإجراءات اللازمة لتنفيذ القرارين. وأوضح مجلس الوزراء أن القرارات تأتي في إطار حرص الدولة على تخفيف أعباء المعيشة وتوفير السلع الأساسية للمواطنين. وكان رئيس مجلس السيادة الانتقالي، الفريق أول ركن عبد الفتاح البرهان، وجّه الأربعاء الماضي برفع الحظر عن استيراد السلع وإعفاء السلع الغذائية الأساسية من الرسوم الجمركية. ورحبت الغرفة القومية للمستوردين بالتوجيهات، وطالبت بترجمتها إلى قرار رسمي وصريح، إلى جانب خفض الدولار الجمركي وإلغاء نظام الإقرار المسبق للشحنات (ACD)، بما يسهم في تيسير إجراءات الاستيراد وتقليل تكلفته. وفي أبريل الماضي، فرض مجلس الوزراء السوداني حظراً على استيراد أكثر من 40 سلعة، وصفها بأنها كمالية وغير ضرورية، في خطوة استهدفت الحد من انفلات سعر الصرف في الأسواق الموازية، وتشجيع الصناعات المحلية ودعم الاقتصاد الوطني. دارفور 0 عناصر من قوات الدعم السريع نيالا 26 أكتوبر 2026 – أعلن مرصد كردفان، الاثنين، وفاة ثلاثة مدنيين كانت تحتجزهم قوات الدعم السريع في سجن دقريس بمدينة نيالا، عاصمة ولاية جنوب دارفور. وقال المرصد، في بيان، إن المتوفين هم معاوية آدم سليمان جبارة، وحسن محمد عبد القادر، وآدم حامد لبن، المعروف بـ«شعيرية»، مشيراً إلى أنهم ينحدرون من محلية غبيش بولاية غرب كردفان، واعتُقلوا في يوليو 2025 خلال حملة نفذتها قوة تابعة للدعم السريع، طالت أكثر من 50 شخصاً آخرين. وأوضح أن المعتقلين نُقلوا إلى مدينة نيالا دون إبلاغ أسرهم بأسباب احتجازهم، مضيفاً أن عائلاتهم ظلت تجهل مصيرهم حتى تلقيها أنباء الوفاة. وأشار البيان إلى أن جبارة كان يعمل في بيع إطارات السيارات بسوق غبيش، بينما عمل عبد القادر في تجارة اللحوم المجففة المعروفة محلياً باسم «الشرموط»، في حين كان لبن معلماً ومربياً شارف السبعين من عمره. وأضاف المرصد أن عبد القادر اعتُقل بعدما سأل القوة التي كانت تقتاد قريبه معاوية عن وجهته، لتأمره بالصعود معه، قبل أن ينتهي به الأمر محتجزاً حتى وفاته داخل السجن. مخاوف على مصير المحتجزين وحذر مرصد كردفان من أن الوفيات الثلاث تأتي ضمن نمط من الحوادث التي أُبلغ عنها سابقاً داخل سجن دقريس، وتشمل وفيات مرتبطة بالجوع والمرض والتعذيب، وفقاً للبيان، مطالباً بالتحقيق في ملابسات وفاة المحتجزين والكشف عن الأسباب الفعلية. وأعرب المرصد عن قلقه إزاء مصير بقية المحتجزين، مشيراً إلى وجود 26 شخصاً من مدينة غبيش لا يزالون رهن الاحتجاز، دون معلومات مؤكدة عن أوضاعهم، في ظل انقطاع التواصل بينهم وبين أسرهم منذ اعتقالهم قبل أكثر من عام. وحمّل البيان قوات الدعم السريع وحكومة «تأسيس» المسؤولية عن سلامة المحتجزين وظروف احتجازهم، مطالباً بتوفير الغذاء والرعاية الطبية اللازمة، وضمان حمايتهم من التعذيب وسوء المعاملة. وشدد على ضرورة الإفراج عن المدنيين المحتجزين تعسفياً، داعياً حكومة «تأسيس» إلى اتخاذ إجراءات عاجلة لمنع وقوع مزيد من الوفيات والانتهاكات في أماكن الاحتجاز الخاضعة لسيطرتها الفعلية. ودعا المرصد إلى فتح تحقيق مستقل في ملابسات وفاة المحتجزين الثلاثة ومحاسبة المسؤولين عن أي انتهاكات تثبت مسؤوليتهم عنها، كما طالب بالسماح للمنظمات الحقوقية والإنسانية المستقلة بزيارة سجن دقريس والتحقق من أوضاع المحتجزين ethiopia.title: Tana Forum Opens in Ethiopia As African Leaders Debate Security and Economic Sovereignty
ethiopia.content: Africa: Tana Forum Opens in Ethiopia As African Leaders Debate Security and Economic Sovereignty - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Tana Forum Opens in Ethiopia As African Leaders Debate Security and Economic Sovereignty 25 October 2026 Nile Post (Kampala) By Kenneth Kazibwe The 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa has opened in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, bringing together African leaders, policymakers and security experts to discuss the continent's peace and security challenges, economic sovereignty and changing geopolitical landscape. The three-day forum, running from October 23 to 25, 2026, is being held under the theme "Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation." It seeks to examine how African countries can strengthen their economies, improve resource governance and develop African-led solutions to conflicts and other security threats. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed welcomed the participating leaders and called for stronger African ownership of continental initiatives, including sustainable financing and greater capacity to determine the continent's development priorities. The discussions come amid growing concerns about external economic dependencies, debt vulnerabilities, competition over natural resources and the impact of geopolitical rivalries on African countries. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Participants are examining how economic policies, institutional capacity and regional cooperation can contribute to lasting peace, with a focus on resource governance, digital infrastructure, monetary sovereignty and the development of regional markets. The forum has attracted several prominent African leaders, including Burundi President Évariste Ndayishimiye, Mozambique President Daniel Francisco Chapo, Kenya's Deputy President Kithure Kindiki and former Sierra Leone President Ernest Bai Koroma. Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama, who chairs the Tana Forum Board, is also among the key figures associated with this year's gathering. The forum provides a platform for political leaders, researchers and other stakeholders to exchange views on the continent's security priorities and approaches to regional cooperation. A key issue on the agenda is the relationship between economic sovereignty and peace. Discussions are exploring how countries can retain more value from their natural resources, strengthen domestic industries and reduce dependence on external markets and financing. The forum's organisers have also highlighted the need for stronger African institutions, better coordination among regional bodies and practical measures to address cross-border security threats. Uganda calls for local value addition Uganda's Minister of Defence, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, who represented President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni at a high-level panel on October 24, called for greater investment in local industries and the retention of Africa's wealth within the continent. Speaking during a discussion titled "From the Margins to the Centre: Building an African Model for Peace and Sovereignty in an Age of Geopolitical Rivalry," Kiwanuka argued that development should be assessed by its contribution to individual prosperity rather than infrastructure growth alone. "Development must lead to individual wealth creation, not just infrastructure," he said. Kiwanuka urged African countries to prioritise domestic processing of raw materials instead of exporting them and subsequently importing finished products at higher costs. "We must prioritise local value addition and stop the loss of value through raw material exports," he said, citing Uganda's copper industry as an example of the challenges associated with exporting raw materials while importing processed products. He argued that stronger intra-African trade and regional markets could help countries retain more economic value, create jobs and reduce reliance on external markets. The discussion also examined how African countries could coordinate their resource policies and economic strategies to strengthen their collective bargaining position in the global economy. The forum's broader agenda links economic transformation to efforts to prevent conflict and strengthen political stability. Participants are considering how debt pressures, unequal participation in global value chains and dependence on external technologies and financing can affect public welfare and undermine confidence in institutions. The African Union has similarly emphasised the importance of effective resource management, domestic financing, regional integration and stronger continental institutions in advancing sustainable peace. In a message delivered at the forum on October 24, the Union's leadership highlighted the need to translate Africa's resource wealth into productive capacity and shared prosperity. The discussions also cover digital transformation, cybersecurity and the development of infrastructure that enables African countries to participate more effectively in the global economy while protecting their strategic interests. Guided by the idea that there are multiple routes to the market, the forum recognises that African countries may pursue different approaches to peace and development while working towards shared continental objectives. ethiopia.content: ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership with Ethiopia - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership with Ethiopia - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us ICRC Reaffirms Commitment to Partnership with Ethiopia 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 26, 2026 (ENA)— The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening its partnership with Ethiopia, commending the humanitarian efforts of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS). During discussions with President Taye Atske Selassie, ICRC Regional Director for Africa Mamadou Sow praised the ERCS for its humanitarian work across the country and emphasized the importance of international humanitarian law and strong leadership in ensuring that essential assistance reaches people in need. President Taye and Mamadou Sow discussed the validity and the importance of international humanitarian law. Sow also commended President Taye for promoting cooperation among key Ethiopian government institutions, including the Ministries of Health, Justice and Defense. He expressed appreciation for the access and acceptance granted to the ICRC in Ethiopia, which enable the organization to carry out its humanitarian operations. Highlighting the importance of collaboration with the ERCS, Sow described the organization as a key partner in implementing programs focused on water, health and food security across Ethiopia. "The Ethiopian Red Cross is a marvelous organization," Sow said. "It's our privileged partner in this country, with whom we work across Ethiopia on water, health, and food security." He also praised the ERCS's extensive volunteer network, describing volunteers as the backbone of the organization and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement. "We are very proud of that partnership because it relies on so many volunteers who are the beating heart of our global movement," Sow added. "We take great pride in their work, as well as the strong support Ethiopia provides to its Red Cross society." © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has reaffirmed its commitment to enhancing its partnership with Ethiopia, recognizing the significant humanitarian contributions of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS). In a meeting with President Taye Atske Selassie, ICRC Regional Director for Africa Mamadou Sow praised the ERCS for its extensive humanitarian efforts throughout the country. The discussions highlighted the importance of international humanitarian law and effective leadership in delivering essential assistance to those in need. Sow commended President Taye for fostering collaboration among various Ethiopian government ministries, which has facilitated ICRC's operations. He emphasized the critical role of the ERCS in implementing programs related to water, health, and food security, describing it as a vital partner. Additionally, Sow acknowledged the invaluable contributions of ERCS volunteers, calling them the backbone of the organization and the broader International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement. The partnership is seen as a source of pride for both the ICRC and Ethiopia. (159 words)

ethiopia.title: At Least 48 Civilians Killed in Weekend Attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia Region, Once Again
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: At Least 48 Civilians Killed in Weekend Attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia Region, Once Again - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: At Least 48 Civilians Killed in Weekend Attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia Region, Once Again Peter Fitzgerald Ethiopia's regions, with Tigray and Amhara in the north, and Oromia further south. 26 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — At least 48 people have been killed and more than 31 others wounded, some severely, in attacks by armed men in Chole and Birbo kebeles of Shirka Woreda, Arsi Zone, in southeastern Oromia, residents who attended the victims' mass funeral told Addis Standard , describing door-to-door killings, looting and the use of heavy weapons. The attacks began on Saturday, 24 October evening, and continued into Sunday morning, 25 October, according to the residents. They said the victims included women, elderly people and at least six children under the age of 15, with many of those killed reportedly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. "Armed men were going door to door shooting and stabbing civilians," one resident said, describing how local residents who had organized nighttime neighborhood watches were overwhelmed by heavily armed attackers carrying AK-47 rifles and other weapons. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The resident said the attacks lasted nearly six hours, leaving communities in the two localities devastated and many survivors too frightened to leave their homes. The second resident said rumors had circulated in nearby towns, including Gobesa, Sire and Kula, two days before the attacks, alleging that "Tsimdo members", were using churches to organize themselves. "No one tries to ask questions. Everyone is passing on information like wildfire," the resident said, adding that the allegations had heightened fear in an area that, according to the account, had not previously experienced comparable violence, even during earlier attacks against Orthodox Christians in nearby localities of Shirka Woreda. The resident also said that local police supported the militias and said the attackers withdrew only after the federal army deployed to the area on Sunday evening. Addis Standard could not independently verify the allegations concerning the rumors, the attackers' affiliations or the role of local security forces. The resident said some people in Sire had prepared a letter on Friday to submit to the town administration, expressing fears about security and requesting protection, but their appeal was "not received in time". "No one is interested to take us seriously," the resident said. Mass burial as residents remain in hiding The first 35 to 37 victims were buried in a mass grave on Sunday, according to the two residents. They said only a small number of people, "overcoming their fear", came out to participate in the burial, while many others remained in hiding. The death toll had reached 48 by the time the residents spoke to Addis Standard earlier today, they said, adding that additional burials were still underway and that some of the wounded were in critical condition. The injured were receiving treatment at hospitals in Gobesa and Shirka, while some had been referred to facilities as far away as Chanco, according to the accounts. The residents also reported the looting of a church in Digelu town and the use of heavy weapons during the attacks. Regional government blames 'Tsimdo' The Oromia Regional Government had not issued a formal statement specifically detailing the weekend attacks at the time of publication. However, regional Communication Bureau head Hailu Adugna gave a brief remark to state media about the loss of life and property damage and attributing the violence to "Tsimdo." Adugna claimed "Tsimdo, facing mounting losses, was attempting to divert the government's attention and expand internal conflict." Hailu did not provide details of the killings, including the number of victims, the circumstances of the attacks or the response by security forces. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church had not issued an official statement on the latest attacks at the time of publication. Several local reports have referred to a newly formed militia structure in the region which is said to operate alongside existing regional security formations. Addis Standard could not independently verify the structure, mandate or chain of command of the reported formation. Attempts to reach the regional government's peace and security and police offices for comment were unsuccessful. Part of a wider pattern of killing in Oromia's Arsi The latest killings add up to years of attacks against civilians, particularly Orthodox Christian communities , in Arsi Zone of Oromia. Previous attacks have resulted in dozens of deaths, displacement and the destruction or looting of religious properties. Between 30 May and 1 June 2026, armed attacks in remote farming communities around Teleta Gebriel in Aseko Woreda killed civilians, displaced hundreds of residents into surrounding forests and resulted in the burning of the historic Teleta Saint Gabriel Church and the looting of Kara Kuftena Medhane Alem Church, according to previous reporting by Addis Standard . On 15 June, Abayneh Tebeqe, a priest serving at Gado Saint Mary Church in Shirka Woreda, was kidnapped from his farm in Mitana Gado and subsequently killed, according to reports published at the time. On 13 August 2024, an attack in Tijo village, Aseko Woreda, left six civilians dead, including a local priest, and three others injured , according to previous Addis Standard reporting. In November and December 2023, separate attacks in Shirka and surrounding areas reportedly killed more than three dozen people, with Orthodox Christian families and worshippers among those targeted. In July 2026, the Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported that at least 432 civilians and four local militia members had been killed in targeted attacks across East Arsi since 2021/2022. The rights group documented killings, kidnappings for ransom and forced displacement, with Orthodox Christian communities disproportionately affected, according to its report. ethiopia.summary: At least 48 civilians were killed and over 31 injured in a series of attacks by armed men in the Oromia region of Ethiopia over the weekend. The violence occurred in Chole and Birbo kebeles of Shirka Woreda, where residents reported door-to-door killings, looting, and the use of heavy weaponry. The attacks began on the evening of October 24 and continued into the following morning, targeting primarily followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, including women and children. Local residents described being overwhelmed by heavily armed attackers, and many survivors remain too frightened to leave their homes. The Oromia Regional Government attributed the violence to a group referred to as "Tsimdo," although details regarding the attackers and the response from security forces remain unclear. This incident is part of a troubling pattern of violence against civilians in the region, particularly targeting Orthodox Christian communities, with previous attacks resulting in significant casualties and destruction.

ethiopia.title: Moyale Clashes Leave Trail of Death, Destruction Across Seven Districts - Tens of Thousands Flee to Kenya
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Moyale Clashes Leave Trail of Death, Destruction Across Seven Districts - Tens of Thousands Flee to Kenya - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Moyale Clashes Leave Trail of Death, Destruction Across Seven Districts - Tens of Thousands Flee to Kenya 26 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Fighting triggered by a dispute over the display of the Somali regional state flag in border city Moyale, a city administered by both Oromia and Somali regions , has spread across seven districts over the weekend, leaving a trail of deaths, injuries and property destruction. Tens of thousands have also fled across the border into Kenya seeking safety. The dispute, which escalated into sustained armed clashes on 22 October, has forced thousands of residents to flee their homes, with burned houses and businesses, disrupted services and growing insecurity on both sides of the Ethiopia-Kenya border. Oromo residents in Kenya's Mandera County have also reported alleged retaliatory attacks linked to the fighting. What began as a dispute over the raising of a flag, initially addressed through discussions among town officials and local elders, has escalated into a wider conflict involving security forces from both regions, heavy machine-gun fire, civilian casualties, the wanton destruction of property, and an intense social media war over competing claims to Moyale's ownership, further inflamed by unverified allegations on both sides. On Sunday, 25 October, a group of Kenyan leaders issued a joint statement warning of a deepening humanitarian and security crisis in the border region, calling for urgent assistance for displaced families and protection for civilians amid fears that the violence could spread further. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn We strongly appeal to our local community members not to harm innocent civilians who live or work in our region a group of Kenyan leaders "We are deeply concerned about the ongoing conflict on the Ethiopian side of the border in Moyale," the statement said, adding that the influx of people seeking refuge in Kenya was "severely straining local infrastructure and resources." The statement was issued by Saku Member of Parliament Dido Ali Rasso, Moyale MP Guyo Wako, Baliti Council of Elders chairperson Waqo Jattani and two aspiring Moyale MPs. Citing media reports, the leaders said more than 50,000 civilians had fled across the border into Marsabit County. That figure was higher than estimates reported separately by Kenyan authorities and humanitarian agencies and could not be independently verified by Addis Standard . The leaders appealed to international partners, nongovernmental organizations and humanitarian agencies to support government efforts to provide food, clean water and shelter to displaced families, many of whom had arrived with few belongings. They also urged residents of Kenya's multiethnic border counties of Marsabit, Wajir and Mandera not to target civilians who live or work in the area but have no involvement in the fighting across the border. "We strongly appeal to our local community members not to harm innocent civilians who live or work in our region," the statement said. "They have no involvement in the conflict taking place across the border." The leaders called on authorities to ensure civilian protection and safe passage and urged security agencies to take all necessary measures to safeguard residents. Fighting spreads across seven districts A resident from the Boolee neighborhood in Moyale told Addis Standard that the fighting, which began following a dispute over the flag and the 18 October killing of 13-year-old girl Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa , had spread to seven districts: Moyale town, Moyale Woreda, Guchii, Dhaas, Waacillee, Areeroo and Gumii Eldalloo. The resident said close-range fighting had continued for three days at several locations in Moyale alone, resulting in deaths and hundreds of injuries. The casualty figures could not be independently established. The unrest began on 18 October following the opening of a Somali regional administrative office and the raising of its flag in Moyale By 22 October, the dispute had escalated into heavy fighting involving Oromia and Somali regional security forces. Clashes and reports of homes and businesses being burned subsequently spread from Moyale to Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero, according to earlier reports by Addis Standard . A second resident told Addis Standard that families had scattered across the Borana countryside and nearby Ethiopian towns, including Dubuluq, Yaballo, Mega and Hiddii Lolla. Others had crossed into Kenya, particularly Marsabit County. Schools had closed, electricity and telecommunications services were disrupted, and many people had fled without adequate food, water or shelter. "The Borana are pastoralists; they do not have other military training," the resident said, expressing concern about the community's vulnerability amid the fighting. Residents who fled to surrounding rural areas were enduring cold nights, hunger, thirst and exposure to the sun, according to accounts from both sides of Moyale. A resident from the Somali-administered side of Moyale who also fled to Kenya said the violence had spread to areas bordering Borana and Garri communities, with homes burned, businesses destroyed and families displaced. The resident said many people had crossed the Laga Seeraa into Kenya and that the number continued to rise as families sought refuge with relatives. "This conflict is not merely an inter-ethnic conflict (between Borana and Garri)," the resident said, alleging that government forces were involved on the Oromia side of the confrontation. The resident also reported that hundreds of injured people were receiving treatment in different locations, including private hospitals in Kenya, but said the scale and geographic spread of the fighting made it difficult to establish an accurate casualty toll. Residents and local security officials from Moyale and Negele Borana disputed allegations that Borana residents were attacking other communities, describing their actions as "self-defense". They said federal security forces failed to intervene in areas where fighting was continuing. Addis Standard could not independently verify these competing accounts or establish the extent of regional security forces' involvement from both sides. Tens of thousands cross into Kenya The Kenya Red Cross reported on 24 October that more than 14,000 Ethiopians had fled into Kenya, with over 10,900 accommodated in six temporary camps and approximately 4,000 staying with relatives and host families. The organization has begun providing emergency assistance to displaced families, including food, shelter materials, clean water and medical support. Its initial response targeted 1,000 households arriving in Kenya, many of them women, children and young people who had crossed the border with few belongings. The scale of displacement continued to rise. On 25 October, the Kenya News Agency reported that approximately 35,000 Ethiopians had sought refuge in Kenya, citing Marsabit County Commissioner Stanley Kamande. Of those, around 15,000 were reportedly staying in camps, while 20,000 had been accommodated within local communities. Humanitarian agencies and local authorities have warned of shortages of food, clean water, sanitation facilities and shelter, placing additional pressure on communities already facing resource constraints. Retaliatory attacks in Mandera The conflict has also heightened insecurity in Mandera County, northeastern Kenya, where Oromo residents from Ethiopia told Addis Standard they feared retaliatory attacks linked to the fighting in Moyale. One resident said that, beginning on 23 October, youths had targeted Oromo residents in response to the violence across the border. The resident alleged that a young Oromo man was killed and his shop looted, while another woman who had lived in Mandera for years was targeted in an attempted killing. "Even though security forces tried to rescue us, we are still facing serious fear ahead," the resident said, adding that security personnel had arrived in Mandera by air from Nairobi following the unrest. "We are still living in hiding wherever we are," the resident said. They have raised concerns that the fighting in Moyale could trigger more retaliatory violence against civilians in neighboring Kenyan communities who have no direct involvement in the conflict. In their Sunday statement, the Kenyan leaders urged communities across Marsabit, Wajir and Mandera to preserve peaceful coexistence and called on authorities to protect residents regardless of their ethnic background. Attempts by Addis Standard to reach Professor Guyo Wako, the Kenyan-side Moyale administrator under Marsabit County, for comment on the displacement and security situation were unsuccessful. Opinion October 26, 2026 Updated: October 26, 2026 Landlocked Ethiopia, Unstable Red Sea, and Geopolitical battle in the Horn of Africa October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Landlocked Ethiopia, Unstable Red Sea, and Strategic battle in the Horn By Metta-Alem Sinishaw Washington, DC Executive Summary Ethiopia currently faces multi-front insurgencies, severe economic distress, and a legitimacy deficit which collectively poses a serious threat to national survival. The insurgencies are manifestations of a much deeper strategic crisis that needs political reconfiguration. Ethiopia’s internal political crisis, its quest for access to the Sea, and the dispute over Nile water resources are increasingly intertwined. Ethiopia’s quest for access to the Sea is a legitimate and pragmatic effort aimed at building regional integration. Dependence of a country with over 130 million people, expanding economy, and asymmetrical military prowess on a single port increases vulnerability and undermines Ethiopia’s industrial aspiration. Although a commercially leased port is required, it represents only a partial solution to meeting the expanding operational needs. As the security of the Red Sea affects Ethiopia much more acutely than any of its neighbors combined, the fundamental geopolitical question Ethiopia seeks to answer is: “why would neighbors resist to offer Ethiopia a naval base while accommodating similar needs of other countries?” As the geographic and demographic center, Ethiopian stability has significant repercussions on its neighbors. Ethiopia’s sudden rhetoric on access to the Sea and rapprochement with sub-state actors has distorted its otherwise valid security demand and angered its neighbors. Egypt capitalized on the tension and forged a tripartite agreement with Eritrea and Somalia to contain Ethiopia. Its continued encirclement will only exacerbate regional insecurity. Ethiopia’s untactful rhetoric brought strategic costs: the US and EU firmly backed Somalia’s territorial integrity while maintaining Ethiopia in its counter-terrorism commitments. While Russia quietly monitors shifting alignments, China views Ethiopian ambition with skepticism to protect its extensive Belt and Road Initiative and avoid a precedent for Taiwan. Amid this friction, Türkiye brokered the Ankara Declaration, in which Somalia recognizes Ethiopia’s right to access the sea in exchange for a firm commitment to Somalian unity. Ethiopia’s domestic stability, infrastructure ambitions, and military capabilities remain deeply tied to Gulf backing. Rivalry between Gulf Royals is splitting the region into two informal and fluid “blocs” that function without legal or institutional mechanisms. On one hand, the UAE Bloc comprises Israel and aligns with Ethiopia, Somaliland, RSF (Sudan) and desires to project forward commercial and maritime power in the Red Sea. Conversely, the Saudi bloc includes Egypt, Türkiye, Qatar, Somalia, SAF, and Eritrea and desires to restrict Red Sea governance exclusively to littoral states and deprive other middle powers from gaining a foothold in the region. Ethiopia’s relations with Eritrea deteriorated following the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. In response to Ethiopian sudden shift in rhetoric on sea outlets, Eritrea forges partnership with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) old guards that considered the Pretoria deal as complete surrender. In the face of narrowing political space and shared threat from the federal government, seven Ethiopian political and armed opposition groups, including the TPLF, Amhara Fano, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) forged the Ethiopian People’s Forces Alliance for Survival. The alliance seeks to overthrow the government and establish an inclusive transitional administration. Despite contradictory ideology and various national orientations, the alliance marks a paradigm shift in the Ethiopian fragmented political landscape. Rebels are suppressing their self-contradictions to avoid horizontal conflicts and pave the way for convergence. With fluid institution and organization, the cohesion and success of the alliance would only be tested through time, especially until after it offers a credible alternative and inclusive political architecture, beyond coordinated military operations. Rivalry of Gulf Royals increases asymmetric backing and strategic vulnerabilities. Collaboration with the UAE enabled Ethiopia to render Egyptian-led encirclement ineffective. Yet intensified insurgencies prompted the withdrawal of Ethiopian peacekeeping forces from Somalia. Political survival forces rebel to become conduit for external geopolitical rivalries. Disrupting rebels’ access to foreign lifeline is the only mechanism to force them towards a compromise. If the war on Iran prolongs, declining Gulf attention will force cash-starved Horn economies to shift their alignment. The ongoing crisis is not a conventional civil war fought to control the capital but more of a critical existential dispute over what kind of state Ethiopia must become. While external powers can offer financial, technological, and military aid, they cannot settle deep-seated domestic political fractures. Winning the internal war will enhance Ethiopian regional posture and attractiveness to powers. Yet there is no military solution to domestic political demands. The federal government may possess the operational reach to suppress specific fronts, but it cannot win the broader political war without genuine institutional reform. Even if the federal government successfully suppresses insurgencies, it may still lose the political war. Conversely, while capable of degrading federal military capacity and capturing strategic hubs, the alliance lacks a cohesive political program to govern. Thus, a negotiated political settlement is needed to restore lasting stability. Ethiopia’s regional posture will be significantly enhanced through internal healing and reconciliation. While a political solution must come from within, heavy reliance of Ethiopian political actors on external support only delays dialogue, in the absence of which the International Community (IC) has a moral responsibility to pressure the fragmented domestic actors into a negotiated compromise. In collaboration with the IC, the US and EU should condition debt-restructuring agreements on verified, inclusive, and genuine political dialogue. The US should encourage Egypt and Ethiopia towards a comprehensive “two waters” framework to deescalate regional crises. Under this framework, Ethiopia would appease Egyptian concern over the Nile and GERD in exchange for a reliably negotiated maritime access to the Red Sea. The US should urgently persuade its key regional allies (Saudi and UAE) to cease fueling regional conflicts and restraint from transactional engagement with non-state and sub-state actors. BRICS should complement international diplomatic efforts. Its New Development Bank could foster South-South cooperation by financing a tripartite Nile Water, Energy, and Food Security Nexus to pacify rivalry between its members, Egypt and Ethiopia. The AU, in cooperation with the UN, should challenge the Saudi-led Red Sea Council to revise its exclusionary “littoral states first” governance model and become inclusive to accommodate the needs of vital non-littoral anchor states. The AU, UN, and IGAD should jointly pressurize Ethiopian political actors to agree on comprehensive Security Sector Reform (SSR) and negotiate a Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration (DDR) transitional compact to integrate and stabilize the state and preemptively mitigate the zero-sum “winner’s dilemma” that threatens Ethiopian and reginal security. 1. Introduction Ethiopia continues fighting multiple insurgencies and the current political architecture could not restore political stability and remain a fundamental structural fault line. Lingering armed confrontations consumes Ethiopian meager economy and poses a severe foreign exchange crisis that led to painful currency devaluation. Unresolved debt restructuring negotiations continue aggravating the security crisis. High youth unemployment and civil unrest directly feed into active insurgencies. The humanitarian crisis remains unabated; millions are internally displaced and millions of others are in urgent need of emergency food. While acute malnutrition surpassed the critical threshold, nine million children are out of school. The government’s increased reliance on military response and dwindling political space further exacerbates grievance and erodes state legitimacy. The 2026 election was conducted amidst active conflicts and omitted key jurisdictions. The National Dialogue Commission excluded dominant political and armed groups. Seven political and rebel groups forged the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival or “alliance for survival” that vowed to topple the incumbent government. Recent explosions around the capital and critical military infrastructures raised questions about the governments’ established supremacy in military technology. Ethiopian sudden quest for a Sea outlet added a new height of tensions with neighbors, unsettled Egypt, and entangled internal actors with external adversarial states. The rivalry between Egypt and Ethiopia over the Nile, GERD and the Red Sea creates geopolitical standoffs. The Horn remains in political turmoil and competition for influence along the Red Sea continues proliferating conflicts. Sudanese civil war, intra-Somali political tensions, and Ethiopia’s insurgencies are interconnected with external proxies. Rival middle powers are using transactional deals to pull Horn of Africa nations into proxy alliances, including alliance with non-state actors to contain their adversaries from within. The deal offers internal dissidents access to adversarial states and critical support. Efforts to resolve Ethiopia’s internal political crisis should not exclusively rely on domestic discontents, changing regional dynamics should be accounted for . This paper attempts to map out Ethiopia’s dominant political fractures and their interplay with neighboring states. It evaluates the impact of global power competition, transactional deals by regional rivals, and the efforts of Ethiopian opposition groups to rescue the country, before outlining a modest strategic way-out. 2. Existential Threat: The New Strategy for Political Dominance The term “existential threat” has become a dominant political buzzword in the Red Sea Region. Egypt considers Ethiopian development efforts on the Nile River as a threat to its existence. Ethiopia believes that the lack of access to the Sea threatens Ethiopian national survival. Djibouti views Ethiopian port diversification policy as a threat against its existence. The Sudanese warring factions accuse each other of threatening Sudan’s survival as polity. Somali views Ethiopian Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Somaliland as unprovoked aggression against its sovereignty and territorial integrity. Eritrea considers Ethiopia’s rhetoric on access to the Sea as a direct threat against its sovereignty. The utilization of existential threat across the region demonstrates the lack of shared regional agenda, shifting alignment, and entanglement with rival foreign states in which one country’s gain is tantamount to another country’s loss. The use and misuse of “existential threat” in the Ethiopian political landscape is even much more nuanced. Political elites’ selective narrative about historical grievance, real or imagined, has transformed political competition into existential threat. Since the politicization of ethnicity as modus operandi, rival political elites portray themselves as defensive while being perceived as offensive by others, making conflict resolutions nearly impossible. Every ethnic group appears to have contradictory memories with varying historical pasts, making it impossible to have a shared collective national memory. Ethnic entrepreneurs perceive losing political control in each group’s territory as equivalent to losing one’s homeland. The fundamental feature that differentiates a genuine existential threat from that of political threat is the evidence based upon which the respective narratives are built. The 1991 victor prescribed ethnocentric arrangement has empowered ethnic groups, promoted vernacular languages, developed local cultures and traditions. However, despite claiming to have redressed historical grievances, the political architecture only shifted and institutionalized inequality and domination. Assigning federating units to a dominant ethnic group intensified victimhood narratives and exacerbated the claim over existential danger when competing for political power. The Ethiopian state currently faces a profound national security dilemma, while the federal government argues that “armed resistance groups threaten national survival,” regional governments counterclaim that “centralization threatens regional autonomy and therefore we must resist.” However, not all existential threat claims are unfounded. For example, persistent atrocities against Amhara and the recent Tigray war made existential politics much more credible. Human Rights Watch documented serious abuse by multiple parties to the conflict which created powerful lessons for every Ethiopian political actor: “If we lose political power, we may eventually lose our physical security” making political compromise harder. If applied, critical analysis could have helped to distinguish between community security, political autonomy, and elite political power competition to identify the scope, extent, and intent of the threat that political elites often present as one and indivisible. Ethnic entrepreneurs view another governance model simply as an existential threat to their own model. Under current arrangement, political programs and policy preferences are not criteria for affinity with political parties and political loyalty remains exclusively dependent on ethnic identity. When each actor is organized politically and militarily to defend itself against the other, the combined effect creates a national security dilemma that forces even groups with contradictory ideology to forge tactical alliances despite lacking a shared national political program. The emergence of “Tsimdo” and alliance for survival follows this pattern. Such alliances remain purely tactical and operational and rarely get strategic height. Therefore, a serious attempt to chart a new political dispensation in Ethiopia must reimagine how the unfolding tactical alliance could be transformed into a veritable national political and security program in which no community feels excluded. 3. Internal Faultlines and vulnerabilities of Contemporary Ethiopia The 2026 National Dialogue Commission deliberation recognized that variation in historical narratives, state building, heritage, institutional design (ethnic vs Unitary), forms of government (religious vs secularism), and loyalties (class vs ethnic) are the fundamental faultlines. The violent insurgencies Ethiopia continues facing today are only manifestations of a much deeper strategic crisis that demand political reimagination and overhaul over state architectures. In the absence of middle ground and compromise, reconfiguration of fundamental state structure remains only desirable. Continued internal disharmony exasperates fragmentation and makes Ethiopia a geopolitical battle ground. Despite the urgency, however, Ethiopian political actors seem to favor zero-sum games. With a growing population of more than 130 million, expanding economy, and asymmetrical military power balance, dependence on a single port increases Ethiopian vulnerability and severely undermines its industrial aspiration. It stresses that denying access to the sea while reaping massive economic benefit by small sized littoral states is inherently unsustainable and unjust. Ethiopia’s sudden and aggressive rhetoric and its controversial dealings with sub-state actors have deeply alienated its neighbors and overshadowed its otherwise valid national interests. Recent Ethiopia’s demand for maritime access is a legitimate and pragmatic path toward regional stability. Lack of favorable response to Ethiopian longstanding predicament will only aggravate regional insecurity. Because Red Sea instability harms Ethiopia more than any of its neighbors combined, temporary commercial leases are simply insufficient. Ethiopia realizes the distinction between commercial and sovereign access and its geopolitical cascading effect. However, it questions why neighboring states failed to offer Ethiopia with a naval base while allowing several other countries. Despite recent calls for peaceful negotiation and dialogue for mutual economic dividend, Ethiopian request remains misconceived and contentious. Immediate neighbors continue viewing Ethiopian positions as an existential threat and establish alliances with the adversaries of Ethiopia and UAE, Ethiopian dominant external enabler. Ethiopia currently stands at a historical crossroad juncture, and its future would be redefined by the following three inextricably linked domestic and regional geopolitical drivers . These dynamics critically determine Ethiopian relations with its neighbors that align with a web of adversarial actors seeking to project influence in the Red Sea region. 1. Accelerating domestic fragmentation isolated and coordinated insurgencies are severely overstretching federal forces, as witnessed by the recent withdrawal announcement of Ethiopian peacekeeping mission from Somalia. Continued failure of the Ethiopian government to harmonize domestic forces will unavoidably exacerbate Ethiopia’s vulnerability and offer regional adversaries with opportunity for aggressive proxy meddling. 2. The Red Sea stalemate Ethiopia’s rhetoric on the Red Sea and framing of permanent, sovereign sea access as a non-negotiable strategic imperative has triggered acute security anxieties among Somalia, Eritrea, and Djibouti and led to shifting regional alignments. Egypt and Saudi are cooperating with other coastal states that view the Red Sea exclusively as littoral states affairs and seek to contain non-coastal states, and 3. The hydrological faultline The completion of GERD and Ethiopia’s continued desire to build three more dams on the Nile River remains an unyielding existential flashpoint for Egypt, and its aggressive move to construct a military and political encirclement of Ethiopia via treaties with Eritrea and Somalia and recently with Sudan. As a credible internal political settlement significantly enhances Ethiopian regional posture, its fragmentation opens doors for meddling. Without a genuine political settlement, Ethiopia will remain in perpetual conflict in which River Nile and the quest for access to the Red Sea serve as catalysts. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is grappling with multiple insurgencies, economic distress, and a legitimacy crisis, threatening its national survival. The country, landlocked and reliant on a single port, seeks maritime access to enhance regional integration and security. This quest has heightened tensions with neighbors, particularly Egypt, which has formed alliances with Eritrea and Somalia to counter Ethiopia's ambitions. The geopolitical landscape is further complicated by rivalries among Gulf states, with the UAE supporting Ethiopia while Saudi Arabia aligns with Egypt and its allies. Amidst this turmoil, seven opposition groups have united to form the Ethiopian People's Forces Alliance for Survival, aiming to overthrow the government. The ongoing conflict is not merely a civil war but a struggle over Ethiopia's identity and governance. A political solution is essential for stability, requiring internal dialogue and external pressure from the international community to facilitate negotiations and reforms. Without genuine political engagement, Ethiopia risks further fragmentation and regional insecurity.

Addis Ababa needs a confident African diplomacy that joins national ambition to regional prosperity The author (Archive) By Mohamud A. Ahmed – Cagaweyne The most consequential victory in diplomacy often comes before negotiations begin: the power to decide what the argument is about. Egypt has long understood this. When the Nile dispute is presented principally as a question of Egyptian survival, Ethiopia’s development arrives in the conversation already under suspicion. A dam becomes a threat before it becomes a source of electricity. An upstream population’s aspirations become a problem for downstream officials to assess. Ethiopia is left explaining why its future should be permitted to advance. This is a profoundly unequal starting point. Egypt’s dependence on the Nile is real, and any responsible settlement must protect its people against serious harm. But dependence does not confer ownership. Historical advantage cannot become perpetual jurisdiction over another country’s economic choices. The weakness in Cairo’s approach emerges whenever a legitimate demand for security expands into an expectation of control. Prime Minister Dr. Abiy Ahmed’s recent remarks at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa offered a constructive foundation for challenging that imbalance. Speaking in Bahir Dar, he placed dependable maritime access within Ethiopia’s long-term security and developmental interests. “For a nation of more than 130 million people, access to the sea is existential,” he said, according to the Ethiopian News Agency’s October 24 report. He also affirmed that Ethiopia would pursue its aspirations through dialogue and mutual benefit. That combination deserves support: clarity about the national interest, coupled with a peaceful method for advancing it. The importance of this argument extends beyond ports. It asks whether Ethiopia’s needs will be treated as enduring realities to accommodate or recurring ambitions to contain. Its population needs reliable electricity, competitive industries, dependable trade routes, and the capacity to withstand external disruption. These requirements will survive changes of government. A regional strategy that assumes Ethiopia can indefinitely absorb the costs of inadequate infrastructure and constrained connectivity mistakes postponed development for permanent acquiescence. National security includes the material foundations of ordinary life. A hospital awaiting equipment, a manufacturer facing uncertain delivery costs, and a farmer seeking access to distant markets all depend upon systems that connect Ethiopia to the world. Abiy’s Tana remarks situated maritime access within that larger concern and linked reliable corridors to African trade and economic opportunity. This provides a persuasive direction for diplomacy: Ethiopia can explain how dependable access would benefit coastal partners, producers and communities along transport routes. Egypt’s leadership should recognize the consistency this demands. A country that asks the world to understand its geographical dependence on the Nile should be prepared to understand Ethiopia’s geographical dependence on transit arrangements. The circumstances differ, but the principle is straightforward. Geography creates vulnerabilities that diplomacy must manage fairly. Cairo weakens its moral authority whenever it seeks broad accommodation for Egyptian necessity while approaching Ethiopian necessity chiefly as a strategic inconvenience. The opening of the ninth Cairo Water Week on October 25 demonstrated Egypt’s sustained capacity to present its priorities internationally. President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi defended downstream security while acknowledging other basin countries’ development rights. sis.gov.eg . That acknowledgment matters. Its practical value, however, depends upon whether upstream development is allowed to alter an unequal distribution of benefits. A right that can be exercised only when existing beneficiaries approve its consequences is precariously close to a privilege granted at their discretion. Cairo’s diplomatic strength lies partly in continuity. Political leaders establish the message; technical institutions elaborate it; diplomats repeat it; conferences and media carry it to wider audiences. Ethiopia should study that discipline. It should also challenge the selective reasoning that can accompany it. The repeated invocation of Egyptian vulnerability does not settle how competing needs should be reconciled. Repetition may establish familiarity, but familiarity is no substitute for an equitable argument. The essential arithmetic is modest: Egypt’s security cannot require Ethiopia’s development to approach zero. Any arrangement built upon that assumption would contain the seeds of its own failure. The basin’s political equation has several populations, several economies and several legitimate claims. A settlement that recognizes only one country’s indispensable needs leaves too many variables outside the calculation. Those excluded interests eventually return as mistrust, resistance and renewed dispute. Ethiopia should therefore begin with the human purpose of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Electricity means a functioning clinic, a productive workshop, a student able to study after sunset and an enterprise capable of expanding. These aspirations deserve the same moral seriousness as downstream concerns. Poverty should never become the invisible baseline against which another country’s security is measured. An Ethiopian household’s exclusion from reliable power is also a deprivation, even when it produces fewer international headlines. At Tana, Dr. Abiy appropriately connected the dam’s achievement to the obligation to deliver reliable electricity, industrial growth, and improved livelihoods. www.ena.et That is the standard Ethiopian leadership should accept. National achievement acquires lasting authority through public benefit. A dam’s significance rests in the opportunities it creates, and Ethiopia’s international case becomes stronger when its domestic performance makes those opportunities visible. Yet a sound Ethiopian argument must examine operational risks rather than assume that a legitimate purpose resolves them. Reservoir management, prolonged drought and downstream planning require evidence and workable cooperation. Ethiopia should support useful information exchange, credible technical assessment and practical procedures for managing disagreement. Such measures demonstrate responsible authority. They also make it harder to turn uncertainty into an unlimited argument against Ethiopian development. Egypt bears a corresponding responsibility: it must distinguish demonstrable risks from demands that preserve its preferred position indefinitely. A request for dependable drought safeguards deserves serious negotiation. An expectation that upstream development must leave every downstream advantage untouched deserves challenge. Existing use matters, but treating it as an immovable ceiling on everyone else’s future would freeze inequality into the rules of cooperation. The United Nations Watercourses Convention provides an important reference through its principles of equitable and reasonable utilization, cooperation and prevention of significant harm. Applying those principles requires attention to relevant law, agreements and circumstances; citing them does not decide every operational dispute. Their broader significance is clear, however: shared water governance requires consideration of multiple interests. It cannot responsibly be reduced to unlimited upstream discretion or permanent downstream predominance. Ethiopia’s strongest response would combine legal precision with scientific openness. Rainfall totals, for example, reveal little without examining seasonality, storage, accessibility and infrastructure. Equally, claims about a dam’s regional benefits require scrutiny of operating conditions. The country should publish credible analysis, acknowledge uncertainty and invite serious examination. Evidence gives diplomacy a foundation that rhetorical escalation cannot supply. Ethiopia does not need to exaggerate its rights to establish that they matter. Maritime access requires the same discipline. Article 125 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea recognizes access and transit rights for landlocked states while requiring agreement on their exercise and protecting transit states’ legitimate interests. It provides a framework for cooperation, not an automatic entitlement to another country’s territory or a particular port. www.un.org Ethiopia can pursue commercial agreements, infrastructure partnerships, leases and dependable transit arrangements through consent. The Prime Minister’s emphasis on dialogue offers the appropriate political foundation. This makes categorical resistance to Ethiopia’s lawful maritime aspirations especially shortsighted. A dependable corridor can generate port revenue, infrastructure investment, employment, and larger markets. The commercial logic is additive: greater Ethiopian activity can enlarge opportunities for coastal economies. Governments should negotiate the distribution of those gains, rather than assume that Ethiopia’s improved access necessarily diminishes their sovereignty. Properly designed agreements can protect both sovereignty and commercial reliability. Recent coordination among Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan warrants careful Ethiopian assessment. Such alignment does not, by itself, prove a covert strategy of destabilization. Nevertheless, any approach that treats constraining Ethiopia as a durable source of regional advantage would be a grave miscalculation. An economically frustrated and politically insecure Horn would offer Egypt little dependable reassurance. Pressure that deepens mistrust can make the cooperation Cairo seeks harder to obtain. Egypt should resist the temptation to treat every Ethiopian gain as an Egyptian loss. That assumption turns diplomacy into a room with narrowing walls. It encourages tactical obstruction while neglecting the larger interest in a capable upstream partner able to negotiate, share information, and implement commitments. Ethiopia’s instability would make those tasks more difficult. Predictability depends upon institutions, and institutions require a viable economic and political foundation. Ethiopia must draw the corresponding lesson at home. National cohesion, accountable government, and administrative competence strengthen external influence. Its citizens deserve institutions that convert national projects into public opportunity and diplomatic commitments into reliable performance. Confidence abroad becomes more credible when supported by competence at home. The defense of Ethiopian interests therefore requires investment in domestic legitimacy alongside forceful international advocacy. It also requires intellectual infrastructure. Ethiopia needs hydrologists who can test scenarios, lawyers who can explain competing obligations, economists who can evaluate corridor arrangements, and scholars who can assess regional developments independently. A credible research institution devoted to Nile cooperation and the Horn’s economic security could contribute substantially. Its value would depend upon transparent methods and freedom to publish inconvenient findings. Scholarship loses authority when its conclusions are assigned in advance. Universities, professional associations, civil society organizations and diaspora specialists should help sustain that effort. Ethiopia should engage the strongest Egyptian arguments, identify weaknesses in its own policies and produce proposals that withstand scrutiny. Knowledge must accumulate across changes of personnel. A country should not have to reconstruct its case whenever a neighboring minister delivers a speech. Tana can support this continuity by connecting African expertise with the practical responsibilities of government. The continental argument must be equally confident. Pan-Africanism cannot mean preserving an inherited hierarchy in which some societies retain established benefits while others are asked to postpone transformation. Nor can it disregard Egyptian vulnerability. Egypt belongs within the African community whose future Ethiopia invokes. A credible African settlement would protect downstream lives while recognizing upstream development as a legitimate and necessary part of continental progress. Dr. Abiy’s Tana remarks deserve support because they connect an enduring Ethiopian priority to dialogue and mutual benefit. Their promise now requires patient negotiation, technically credible proposals, and agreements that partners can trust. Ethiopia should build upon that foundation to present a coherent regional vision: electricity that supports production, corridors that sustain commerce, and institutions that make cooperation dependable. Cairo can help shape that future, but it must reconsider an approach that too readily confuses Ethiopian advancement with Egyptian danger. The Nile cannot become a permanent instrument for rationing another nation’s aspirations. Ethiopia, for its part, should defend its interests with the confidence to negotiate and the discipline to make its proposals credible. Egypt’s water security deserves protection. Ethiopia’s development deserves room to advance. A durable settlement must be built around both realities. About the Author Mohamud A. The index places Ethiopia at position 90 globally, alongside countries including Somalia, Yemen, Syria and Afghanistan, according to the report cited by Passport Rank. Ethiopian citizens can access a further 33 destinations through visas on arrival, while only five African Union member states -- Kenya, Benin, The Gambia, Rwanda and Togo -- are listed as allowing them visa-free entry. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The ranking reflects the restrictions Ethiopian travelers face when seeking to cross borders, with advance visa applications, extensive documentation and processing delays potentially complicating international travel. These barriers can affect businesses seeking to attend trade exhibitions, negotiate deals or build partnerships abroad, as well as students and researchers pursuing academic exchanges and other international opportunities. The report attributes the passport's low standing to a combination of economic conditions, security concerns and diplomatic relations. It says foreign governments commonly consider income levels, security risks, and the likelihood of visa overstays when determining entry requirements. Regional instability and security concerns in the Horn of Africa are also cited as factors contributing to strict visa screening for Ethiopian travelers. The report further points to limited reciprocal visa-waiver arrangements as a constraint on mobility. The restrictions can create challenges for Ethiopian companies seeking to expand internationally, particularly where foreign businesspeople can enter Ethiopia through e-visas or visas on arrival while Ethiopian nationals must undergo more demanding visa procedures to visit potential markets. The report says the consequences extend beyond commerce to academic cooperation, cultural exchanges, and international engagement. Read the original article on Capital FM .
